Title: Beyond willingness to donate: a cross-sectional online survey to understand urgent blood-donor mobilisability among digitally reachable adults in Ghana
Authors: Shen, H.; Agorinya, I. A.; Ayanore, M. A.; Brede, M.; Chapman, A.; Head, M.
Abstract: ObjectivesTo identify factors associated with anticipated engagement in urgent blood-donor mobilisation among digitally reachable adults in Ghana.  BackgroundDigital tools may facilitate contact with potential blood donors during emergencies and blood shortages, but digital reachability does not ensure engagement with urgent requests.  MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional online survey across Ghanas 16 regions (September 2025-January 2026), recruiting participants via Facebook advertising and snowball sampling. Factors associated with urgent blood-donor mobilisability were assessed under four criteria: future-donation willingness; willingness to install a trusted donation app; willingness to respond to a trusted urgent-request; and practical flexibility to leave current activities. Descriptive analyses and multivariable logistic regression examined prevalence and associated factors.  ResultsOf 1,067 respondents, 577 (54.1%) met all four criteria, compared with 91.8% reporting high future-donation willingness. Trusted-app installation willingness (83.2%) and trusted-request response willingness (82.7%) exceeded practical flexibility (66.6%). High mobilisability was associated with formal health-system trust (AOR 3.95, 95% CI 2.08-7.50), digital-response readiness (AOR 2.26, 1.66-3.08), donation knowledge (AOR 1.42, 1.03-1.97) and previous donation (AOR 1.47, 1.08-2.01). Women (AOR 0.60, 0.43-0.83), those with work-schedule barriers (AOR 0.43, 0.29-0.66) and those reporting >30-minute night-time travel to the nearest healthcare facility (AOR 0.66, 0.45-0.96) had lower adjusted odds.  ConclusionsDigital reachability and stated donation willingness may overestimate the population pool available for emergency donation. Digital blood-donor solutions should consider verifiable health-system requests, account for digital-response readiness and current availability, and connect willing individuals with accessible collection options and transport support where needed.

Title: Adult disability and mental/psychological illness in Somaliland socioeconomic inequalities and co-occurrence in the 2020 Somaliland Health and Demographic Survey
Authors: Saed, A. A.; Osman, O. A.; Adan, A. M.; Suleiman, Y. I.; Mohamed, A. I.
Abstract: Disability is an important population-health concern, but adult-specific evidence on its distribution and socioeconomic patterning remains limited in Somaliland. This study estimated the prevalence and distribution of reported disability among adults in Somaliland and examined socioeconomic inequality, reported mental/psychological illness, and their co-occurrence.  We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of the 2020 Somaliland Health and Demographic Survey. The analysis included 14,579 adults aged >18 years who were usual residents, had the disability module administered, and had a defined reported mental/psychological illness measure. Reported disability was defined as at least one positive response across seven disability domains: sight, hearing, speech, learning, mobility, self-care, and mental. Survey-weighted prevalence estimates and design-based comparisons were calculated. Survey-weighted logistic regression assessed associations with household wealth and other covariates. Socioeconomic inequality was assessed using a concentration index and the normalized Erreygers concentration index. Co-occurrence was evaluated by comparing observed joint prevalence with that expected under statistical independence and by survey-weighted logistic regression.  The survey-weighted prevalence of any reported disability was 7.30% (95% CI 6.65-8.02). Sight was the most frequently reported domain (3.83%, 95% CI 3.19-4.59), followed by hearing (1.54%, 95% CI 1.20-1.97) and mobility (1.39%, 95% CI 1.14-1.70). Disability prevalence increased markedly with age, from 4.15% among adults aged 18-29 years to 23.96% among those aged >60 years. The crude wealth pattern was non-monotonic and was not statistically detectable after adjustment for residence and region. The concentration index for reported disability was 0.0584 (SE 0.0284, p=0.0415). Reported mental/psychological illness had a weighted prevalence of 0.71% (95% CI 0.50-1.00). Both reported disability and reported mental/psychological illness occurred in 0.5032% of adults, compared with 0.05185% expected under statistical independence; the observed-to-expected ratio was 9.70 (95% CI 7.60-11.81). After adjustment for age group and sex, reported disability was strongly associated with reported mental/psychological illness (OR 42.99, 95% CI 18.45-100.18).  Reported disability affected approximately one in fourteen adults in Somaliland and showed a marked age gradient and substantial geographic variation. The crude socioeconomic pattern was attenuated after adjustment for geographic context, while concentration analysis indicated modest marginal concentration toward higher wealth ranks. Reported mental/psychological illness was uncommon but co-occurred with reported disability more often than expected under independence. These findings provide an adult population baseline for Somaliland while highlighting the need to distinguish survey-reported disability from the separate mental/psychological illness construct and to interpret the findings within the limitations of cross-sectional, survey-reported measures. O_LIEvidence on disability among adults in Somaliland is limited, especially on its socioeconomic distribution and relationship with reported mental/psychological illness. C_LIO_LIWe used the 2020 Somaliland Health and Demographic Survey to examine these patterns nationally. C_LI What did the researchers do and find? O_LIWe analysed 14,579 adults aged 18 years or older using survey-weighted methods that accounted for the surveys sampling design. C_LIO_LIOverall, 7.30% of adults reported at least one disability domain. Sight, hearing, and mobility were most frequently reported, and disability was much more common among older adults and varied across regions and residence settings. C_LIO_LIReported mental/psychological illness was found in 0.71% of adults. Both conditions occurred together in 0.50%, substantially more than expected under statistical independence. C_LI What do these findings mean? O_LIOur study provides an adult population baseline for reported disability in Somaliland and shows clear differences by age and geographic context. C_LIO_LIOur findings highlight the importance of keeping reported disability and reported mental/psychological illness as distinct measures. C_LIO_LIBecause our data are cross-sectional and based on reported survey measures, the findings describe the 2020 survey period and do not establish clinical diagnoses or causal relationships. C_LI

Title: Interactions between respiratory viruses in US adults and children: a prospective cohort study
Authors: Hoffman, K. L.; Weil, A. A.; Wetzler, E. A.; Akinola, B. O.; Beauge, A.; Andy, C.; Adams, A.; Frivold, C.; Cox, S. N.; Ehmen, B.; Hatchie, T.; Clark, E. L.; Drummond, M.; Englund, J.; Han, P. D.; Kuntz, J. L.; Lo, N. C.; Lockwood, C.; Starita, L.; Mularski, R. A.; Naleway, A. L.; Carone, M.; Chu, H. Y.
Abstract: BackgroundThe relationship between recent viral infection and subsequent susceptibility to, or protection against, other viruses remains unclear, particularly across age groups and symptom status.  MethodsA prospective cohort study enrolled participants aged 6 months to 49 years in Washington and Oregon, USA, 2022-2024. Weekly nasal swabs were tested for SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and influenza A/B; additional swabs were collected during symptomatic illness and were also tested for parainfluenza (PIV) 1-4, endemic human coronaviruses (hCOV), adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, human rhinovirus (hRV), and enteroviruses. Proportional hazards regression models were used to characterize associations between incident symptomatic infection (illness) and history of recent illness due to other viruses (within 1-7, 8-14, 15-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-180 days), adjusted for geographic region, age, sex, daycare/school/work attendance, household size, and number of children in the household. For SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and RSV, these analyses were repeated to study incidence of infection (including asymptomatic cases).  FindingsOf 3,560 participants, 2,969 (83%) had [≥]1 illness over 4,299 person-years. Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) in the short term ([≤]2 weeks) after an illness were predominantly below 1, indicating that recent viral illness was often associated with lower risk of subsequent illness with other viruses. Across age groups, recent hRV illness was associated with lower risk of hCOV, PIV, and RSV illness (aHRs 0.07-0.27). SARS-CoV-2 illness was associated with a higher short-term risk of adenovirus and PIV illness (aHRs 3.20-3.33). In children aged 6 months-4 years, recent influenza illness was associated with higher short-term risk of SARS-CoV-2 illness. Including asymptomatic infections generally attenuated these associations.  InterpretationSome viral illnesses may alter short-term susceptibility to subsequent viral illnesses. Interactions may differ by age and symptom status.  FundingUS Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; Washington State Department of Health.

Title: Exploratory network-based modelling of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease importation and spread in Uganda using Displacement Tracking Matrix flow data
Authors: Walekhwa, A. W.; Mbaka, P.; Nannyonga, B. K.; Silal, S. P.; Bbuye, M.; Magoba, B.; Nakiire, L.; Lamorde, M.; Sulaimon, T. A.; Kwesiga, B.; Sabiiti, W.; Mutamba, W.; Turinawe, G.; Nakazibwe, B.; Kayiwa, J.; Nantongo, M.; Ipola, P. A.; Kungu, P.; Ario, A. R.; Kagirita, A.; Lubwama, B.; Kirenga, B. J.; Wayengera, M.; Muruta, A. N.; Olaro, C.; Atwine, D.
Abstract: BackgroundThe 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in Uganda, linked to the ongoing epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), spread through human mobility across borders and within the country. Existing modelling has provided regional-level importation estimates but not district-level operational guidance. We developed an exploratory, scenariobased decision-support model to characterise subnational importation and spread patterns.  MethodsWe constructed a directed, weighted mobility network using International Organization for Migration (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) flows collected from 15-24 May 2026 (11,245 observed movements) and the 2024 Uganda census. A stochastic metapopulation SEIR model was simulated over 90 days across 135 Ugandan districts and two DRC provinces. We evaluated three scenario assumptions--containment (R0 = 0.80), moderate (R0 = 1.35), and weak (R0 = 2.76)--plus a one-factor-at-a-time analysis of nonpharmaceutical intervention (NPI) compliance. Global sensitivity analysis was performed using Morris elementary-effects screening and total-order Sobol indices.  ResultsThe mobility network was sparse (density 0.11), highly unequal (Gini 0.67), and modular (0.50). Kisoro had the highest import risk (in-strength 3,823) and export risk (outstrength 1,350). Under all three scenarios, the model projected similar cumulative case counts (median 20-21; pairwise Mann-Whitney p < 0.05). Under containment, Kampala was the only district with a non-zero median (20 cases, 95% simulation interval 20-22); all other districts had median 0. Prediction-interval coverage against the early observed curve was 0.80.  ConclusionsUnder the models containment assumptions, rapid 7-1-7 implementation was associated with substantial containment, but this is scenario-specific and does not imply that NPIs are unnecessary. Border surveillance, nationwide preparedness, and community engagement remain essential. These projections should be treated as exploratory and require prospective field-based validation.

Title: Pharmacovigilance and Mechanistic Analysis of Adverse Reaction Differences Across EGFR Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Generations in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
Authors: Arojo, O.; Jones, A. M.
Abstract: BackgroundEpidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are widely used for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) but have distinct toxicity profiles across generations.  AimsTo investigate relationships between EGFR-TKI physicochemical, pharmacokinetic and pharmacological properties and drug-specific adverse drug reactions (ADRs) using national and global pharmacovigilance data.  MethodsADRs for erlotinib, afatinib and osimertinib were extracted from the UK MHRA Yellow Card scheme and WHO VigiAccess. Disproportionality analysis used reporting odds ratios (RORs). Signals were defined as ROR [≥]2, lower 95% confidence interval >1 and [≥]3 cases. Drug properties were curated from ChEMBL, emc, SmPC and EMA sources.  ResultsVigiAccess contained 88,662 individual case safety reports (163,619 ADRs) and Yellow Card contained 752 reports (1,814 ADRs). Four System Organ Class (SOC) signals were identified in VigiAccess and three in Yellow Card, with five additional Yellow Card Preferred Term signals. Eye disorders showed the strongest consistent association with erlotinib (VigiAccess ROR 4.33; Yellow Card ROR 4.18). Osimertinib was associated with pneumonitis (ROR 7.67) and pulmonary embolism (ROR 3.94). Afatinib showed psychiatric disorder signals in both databases (ROR 3.2- 3.3) and diarrhoea (ROR 2.79). Neoplasm-related signals likely reflected confounding by indication.  ConclusionsEGFR-TKIs demonstrate generation-specific pharmacovigilance profiles. Integration with drug properties supports mechanistic plausibility for several signals, while the atypical afatinib psychiatric association warrants further investigation. Findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in controlled observational or mechanistic studies.  What is already known about this subject?O_LIFirst-, second-and third-generation EGFR-TKIs (erlotinib, afatinib and osimertinib) are established treatments for EGFR-mutated NSCLC but are associated with distinct adverse drug reaction (ADR) profiles that differ across generations. C_LIO_LIKnown class-effect toxicities include dermatological, gastrointestinal, and ocular ADRs, attributed to EGFR inhibition in non-tumour epithelial tissues. C_LIO_LIPrior pharmacovigilance studies using the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) have characterised EGFR-TKI safety signals, but UK-specific Yellow Card data have not been systematically analysed across all three generations, and the pharmacological basis for generation-specific differences remains incompletely understood. C_LI  What this study addsO_LIDual-database disproportionality analysis of MHRA Yellow Card and WHO VigiAccess data, using a pre-specified signal threshold (ROR [≥] 2, lower 95% CI > 1, n [≥] 3), confirmed generation-specific signals: eye disorders for erlotinib; psychiatric disorders and diarrhoea for afatinib; and pneumonitis and pulmonary embolism for osimertinib. C_LIO_LIIntegration of target potency (pIC50), ErbB family selectivity, blood brain barrier (BBB) penetration and CYP450 interaction data with the pharmacovigilance signals provides mechanistic plausibility, linking them to variations in binding reversibility, wild-type EGFR inhibition, and off-target kinase activity. C_LIO_LIApplying a pre-specified, conservative signal threshold distinguished genuine disproportionate signals from elevated but non-significant reporting and identified neoplasm-related findings as confounded by indication rather than true drug safety signals highlighting the importance of rigorous signal definition in oncology pharmacovigilance. Title: Impact of air pollution and tobacco smoke on the placental small non-coding RNA landscape
Authors: Falcon-Gracia, A.; Vespalcova, H.; Peligri, D.; Aguilar-Lacasana, S.; Pantano, L.; Nurtdinov, R. N.; Garcia, Z.; Dominguez, A.; Gomez-Herrera, L.; Sanchez, O.; Gascon, M.; Foraster, M.; Guigo, R.; Llurba, E.; Gomez-Roig, M. D.; Rivas, I.; Dadvand, P.; Sunyer, J.; Bustamante, M.; Cosin-Tomas, M.
Abstract: Fetal development is highly sensitive to environmental influences, including maternal smoking during pregnancy (MSDP) and air pollution. The placenta may play a central role in mediating these effects through epigenetic mechanisms, including small non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs). While most studies have focused on microRNAs (miRNAs), other sncRNA classes remain poorly characterized. Here, we characterized the placental sncRNA landscape and investigated its associations with prenatal exposure to MSDP and air pollution.  The sncRNA expression profile of 390 chorionic villi samples from the Barcelona Life Study Cohort (BiSC) was measured using small RNA sequencing and the seqBuster/seqCluster pipeline. MSDP was assessed via questionnaire, and prenatal exposure to black carbon (BC), particulate matter [≤]2.5 m (PM2.5), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was estimated using hybrid dispersion-land-use regression (LUR) spatiotemporal models. Associations were evaluated using linear regressions adjusted for relevant covariates.  We identified 979 placental sncRNA clusters, assigned primarily to miRNAs (33.2%), piRNAs (26.4%), snoRNAs (12.2%), tRFs (7.8%), and others (20.4%). MSDP was associated with the downregulation of miR-421 and the upregulation of multiple snoRNAs from the imprinted DLK1-DIO3 locus (SNORD113-4, SNORD114-2, SNORD114-3, and SNORD114-17), as well as the piR-26394. No sncRNAs remained significantly associated with air pollution after multiple-testing correction, although several miRNAs showed suggestive associations.  Overall, this study provides a comprehensive characterization of placental sncRNAs and identifies previously unreported smoking-associated sncRNAs within the imprinted DLK1-DIO3 locus, expanding our understanding of placental epigenetic responses to prenatal environmental exposures.

Title: Metabolic Control and the Symptoms/Problems Domain of Kidney Disease-Specific Quality of Life in Patients Receiving Kidney Replacement Therapy
Authors: Moran-Ramos, D.
Abstract: BackgroundHealth-related quality of life (HRQoL) is an important outcome in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) receiving kidney replacement therapy (KRT), but the relationship between comprehensive metabolic control and the Symptoms/Problems domain of kidney disease-specific HRQoL remains uncertain.  ObjectiveTo evaluate the association between composite metabolic control and the Symptoms/Problems domain of the Kidney Disease Quality of Life-36 (KDQOL-36) in patients with stage 5 CKD receiving KRT, and to explore the relationship between individual metabolic parameters and the continuous Symptoms/Problems score.  Materials and MethodsWe conducted an observational, cross-sectional, analytical study of 177 adults receiving hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis at a nephrology unit in Chihuahua, Mexico. Metabolic control included blood pressure, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), total cholesterol, and triglycerides. Adequate control was defined as achievement of at least three of four study-defined operational thresholds. The KDQOL-36 Symptoms/Problems score was analyzed as a continuous variable and categorized as low, moderate, or high according to the study protocol. Group comparisons, Spearman correlations, Pearson chi-square tests, and ordinal logistic regression were performed.  ResultsAdequate metabolic control was present in 106 patients (59.9%). No, statistically significant association was observed between achievement of at least three of four study-defined operational thresholds and Symptoms/Problems score category ({chi}2=3.983; p=0.137; Cramers V=0.150). None of the individual metabolic parameters differed significantly across Symptoms/Problems score categories or showed significant correlations with the continuous score. In ordinal logistic regression, adequate metabolic control yielded an odds ratio of 1.81 (95% CI: 0.98-3.35; p=0.057) after adjustment for age, sex, time receiving KRT, and KRT modality.  ConclusionsNo, statistically significant association was identified between the operational definition of metabolic control used in this study and the KDQOL-36 Symptoms/Problems domain in patients with stage 5 CKD receiving KRT. The findings support evaluating HRQoL multidimensionally and warrant confirmation in larger longitudinal studies.  CategoriesFamily/General Practice, Internal Medicine, Nephrology

Title: Variation in psychiatric diagnoses and use of psychotropic medication among children, adolescents, and young adults in Denmark
Authors: Sonne, H.; Kildegaard, H.; Bech, M.; Wesselhoeft, R.; Hansen, A. S. K.; Ording, A. G.; Pottegaard, A.
Abstract: BackgroundPsychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use among children, adolescents, and young adults have increased in high-income countries, with concerns about geographic variation. We described national trends and geographic variation in Denmark from 2010 to 2025 and developed an interactive online tool to explore these patterns.  MethodsWe conducted a nationwide, descriptive, repeated cross-sectional register-based study of all Danish residents aged 0-24 years in 2010-2025 (n=2,930,744), using the Danish National Patient Registry and the Danish National Prescription Registry. We estimated annual incidence, prevalence, and, for selected diagnoses, lifetime prevalence, by age and sex, and age- and sex-standardised rates across regions, health councils, and municipalities. We assessed geographic variation using deviations from national means, coefficients of variation, Gini coefficients, and funnel plots.  FindingsPsychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use increased from 2010 to 2025. The annual prevalence of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) increased from 0{middle dot}41 to 2{middle dot}3 per 100 individuals, autism spectrum disorders from 0{middle dot}20 to 1{middle dot}2, and melatonin use from 0{middle dot}14 to 3{middle dot}0. ADHD and autism spectrum disorders were more prevalent among boys and anxiety disorders among girls. Sertraline use was also more prevalent among girls. Geographic variation was observed across diagnoses and psychotropic medications at regional, health council, and municipal levels. For example, lifetime prevalence of autism ranged from 1{middle dot}3 to 5{middle dot}9 per 100 across municipalities, and in 2025 regional coefficients of variation ranged from 0{middle dot}11 (sertraline) to 0{middle dot}41 (atomoxetine). Results can be explored in the interactive online tool (https://bupstat.sdu.dk/?lang=en).  InterpretationPsychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use increased among Danish children, adolescents, and young adults, with marked geographic variation. Descriptive data cannot establish the causes of this variation, but the findings identify areas for further review and support continued monitoring.  FundingBest for Us project (www.bedstforos.dk), funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF24SA0093635) and the Obel Family Foundation (69348).  Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed on 25 September 2026 without date or language restrictions, using two search strings (Appendix Text 1). One search string combined search terms for psychiatric disorders and psychotropic medications, children, adolescents, and young adults, and geographic variation. The other search string combined similar population and condition terms with time trends and Denmark or other Nordic countries. We supplemented these with reference lists of key publications, health atlas websites, and national reports. Existing evidence shows substantial increases in psychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use among children and adolescents in high-income countries over the past two decades, with particularly marked rises in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorders, and use of ADHD medications, antidepressants, and melatonin. Studies show considerable geographic variation in diagnostic and prescribing practices that differences in underlying morbidity cannot fully account for. Other countries have produced health atlases examining geographic variation in child and adolescent mental healthcare. However, no comparable nationwide analysis covering both psychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use across multiple geographic levels has previously been conducted in Denmark. The identified studies were predominantly observational and register-based. Nationwide health registries provide high-quality data, but the observational nature limits causal inference about the mechanisms underlying the observed variation.  Added value of this studyThis study provides the first nationwide, comprehensive mapping of both psychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use among Danish children, adolescents, and young adults over a 16-year period. By applying standardised measures of geographic variation, including coefficients of variation, Lorenz curves, and Gini coefficients, across a broad range of diagnostic categories and medication groups simultaneously, this study extends previous Danish and Nordic work. The accompanying interactive online tool enables dynamic exploration of temporal and geographic patterns and supports ongoing monitoring and dissemination of findings beyond the research community.  Implications of all the available evidenceThe substantial geographic variation observed across diagnostic and prescribing practices, combined with the rising prevalence of psychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use, highlights the need for continued monitoring of child and adolescent mental healthcare in Denmark. The findings provide a foundation for targeted quality-improvement initiatives, resource planning, and closer alignment of diagnostic and prescribing practice at the regional and municipal levels. Future research should examine the mechanisms underlying geographic variation, including the role of access to services, local clinical cultures, and socioeconomic factors, and evaluate the impact of initiatives to reduce unwarranted variation.

Title: Heart rate rises most during REM sleep after semaglutide initiation: a matched longitudinal cohort study
Authors: Krongauz, D.; Kohn, S.; Zulti, A.; Schlesinger, Y.; Godneva, A.; Talmor-Barkan, Y.; Segal, E.
Abstract: Study Objectives.Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists raise resting heart rate. We asked whether, after semaglutide initiation, the increase is larger during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep than during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.  Methods.In the Human Phenotype Project, an Israeli cohort of generally healthy adults aged 40 to 70 years, 96 of 494 self-reported semaglutide initiators had a home sleep study (WatchPAT; sleep stages estimated from peripheral arterial tone and actigraphy) before and at least three months after starting. Each was propensity-matched 1:1 to a never-user of GLP-1 drugs measured at the same visits. We estimated the initiators change minus their controls change (difference-in-differences). The REM minus NREM contrast was designated primary after an exploratory analysis.  Results.Relative to controls (90 to 94 pairs), heart rate rose during nocturnal wake (+3.89 beats per minute [bpm], 95% confidence interval 2.35 to 5.44), NREM sleep (+4.82 bpm, 3.12 to 6.52) and REM sleep (+6.25 bpm, 4.42 to 7.91); the REM increase exceeded the NREM increase by 1.42 bpm (0.98 to 1.89). The excess persisted across matching designs and on a relative scale; the proportion of REM sleep did not change. Never-users with similar weight loss showed no REM sleep heart-rate rise (+0.40 bpm, -0.63 to 1.50). Heart-rate variability decreases disappeared after adjustment for heart rate.  Conclusions.Semaglutide initiation was associated with higher heart rate throughout sleep, most during REM sleep, unexplained by weight loss. Clinic measurements may understate this effect. Confirmation with polysomnographic staging is needed. Whether it differs between sleep stages has not been formally tested. After people started semaglutide, heart rate rose in every sleep stage estimated by a home sleep apnea test, most during rapid eye movement sleep; weight loss did not explain it. A higher sleeping heart rate on a wearable after starting the drug may therefore be an expected effect, not illness. Whether the rise matters for patients with heart disease, in whom rapid eye movement sleep can provoke ischemia and arrhythmia, requires prospective studies with dispensed exposure and electroencephalographic sleep staging.

Title: Documented Dental Disease in Patients With Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia
Authors: Ssentongo, P.; Peacock, W. F.; Durieux, J. C.; Colovos, C.
Abstract: ImportanceClinicians often look for a dental source in Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB), but how often dental disease is found, compared with other bacteremias, is unclear.  ObjectiveTo compare documented dental disease in adults with SAB, Escherichia coli bacteremia, and a general population cohort.  Design, Setting, and ParticipantsRetrospective cohort study in the Protege database of 48 975 adults with bacteremia from January 1, 2015, through December 31, 2023, assigned by earliest in-window organism, and 81 945 general population adults.  ExposuresSAB, with E coli bacteremia as the primary comparator and the general population as the secondary comparator.  Main Outcomes and MeasuresDocumented dental disease from 7 days before through 30 days after index, defined by a qualifying dental procedure or disease-specific note text and adjusted for age, sex, race, and documentation intensity.  ResultsDental disease occurred in 528 of 16 435 patients with SAB (3.21%) and 179 of 24 942 patients with E coli bacteremia (0.72%). The adjusted odds ratio was 3.86 (95% CI, 3.23 to 4.63). By the pathology-only definition, disease occurred in 517 patients with SAB (3.15%) and 399 general population patients (0.49%). The adjusted odds ratio was 3.71 (95% CI, 3.08 to 4.46). Within SAB, rates were highest with prior infective endocarditis (9.8%), opioid use disorder (6.2%), injection drug use (5.3%), and prosthetic valve (5.0%). Prevalence ranged from 0.49% in the general population to 7.98% in other streptococcal bacteremia. Of 437 patients with SAB and an assignable first finding date, 333 (76.2%) had the finding after the index date.  Conclusions and RelevanceDental disease was documented more often in SAB than in E coli bacteremia after adjustment. Most findings were first recorded after bacteremia was recognized, during SAB evaluation. These data do not show that dental disease caused the bacteremia.  Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSIs dental disease documented more often in Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB) than in Escherichia coli bacteremia or a general-population cohort?  FindingsIn 16 435 adults with SAB and 24 942 with E coli bacteremia, documented dental disease occurred in 3.21% and 0.72%, respectively. The adjusted odds ratio was 3.86 (95% CI, 3.23 to 4.63). Among SAB patients with an assignable date, 76.2% had the first finding after the index date.  MeaningDental disease was documented more often with SAB than with a nonoral bacteremia. This supports focused oral assessment during source evaluation, but does not establish the mouth as the source.

Title: Development and Validation of a Parsimonious Financial Well-Being Index in the Health and Retirement Study
Authors: Habib, M. H.; Mayeda, E. R.; Barry, L.; Arah, O. A.; Nau, C. L.; Zhou, H.; Kezios, K. L.; Nianogo, R. A.
Abstract: Unstructured AbstractFinancial well-being (FWB) encompasses objective and subjective financial status and may influence health. We developed and validated a parsimonious FWB index using data from 23,006 Health and Retirement Study (HRS) participants aged [≥]50 years during 2006-2022. The FWB-5 Index was derived using correlated two-factor confirmatory factor analysis accounting for household clustering. Indicators included household wealth, household income-to-poverty ratio, monthly financial strain, satisfaction with ones financial situation, and perceived financial mastery. We assessed convergent and discriminant validity using the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Financial Well-Being (CFPB-FWB) Scale and Satisfaction with Life Scale, respectively. Associations with pre-baseline socioeconomic factors and subsequent depressive symptoms and health conditions were examined to assess construct and predictive validity. Model fit indices supported the two-factor structure (robust comparative fit index = 0.99; robust root mean square error of approximation = 0.05). Correlations were stronger with the CFPB-FWB Scale (Spearman {rho} = 0.80) than with life satisfaction ({rho} = 0.43). Associations with socioeconomic factors and subsequent health outcomes were in the hypothesized directions. These findings support the FWB-5 Index as a parsimonious measure for examining financial well-being and its associations with health across HRS waves, including those predating the CFPB-FWB Scale.

Title: Effects of a 500-day LPG cookstove and fuel intervention delivered during gestation and infancy on height-for-age (HAZ) and stunting at ages 2, 3, 4 and 5 years: findings from a follow-up study of the multi-country HAPIN trial
Authors: Kalam, M. A.; Sinharoy, S. S.; Steenland, K.; Thompson, L. M.; Diaz-Artiga, A.; McCracken, J. P.; Balakrishnan, K.; Aravindalochanan, V.; Garg, S.; Rosa, G.; Ndagijimana, F.; Jabbarzadeh, S.; Johnson, M.; Pillarisetti, A.; Kearns, K.; Lovvorn, A. E.; Ramakrishnan, U.; Peel, J.; Clasen, T. F.
Abstract: ObjectiveReducing household air pollution exposure during gestation and infancy may have longer-term benefits for child linear growth. We examined whether a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cookstove and fuel intervention delivered during gestation and infancy could improve height-for-age Z scores (HAZ) and reduce the risk of stunting at ages 2-5 years in India, Rwanda, and Guatemala.  Materials and methodThe Household Air Pollution Intervention Network (HAPIN) was a randomized controlled trial that enrolled [~]3200 pregnant women across Guatemala, India, Peru, and Rwanda. Women in the intervention group received an LPG cookstove and free fuel during pregnancy and until the infant reached 12 months of age. Following the HAPIN trial, we continued following children in Guatemala, India, and Rwanda (N=2169) and measured child height at ages 2, 3, 4, and 5 years (HAPIN 2.0). As prespecified in the study protocol, we used mixed-effects models, as well as linear and log-binomial regression, within the intention to treat (ITT) framework, to evaluate the interventions effect on HAZ and stunting. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess effect modification by child sex, maternal height, and intervention country.  ResultsThe intervention reduced gestational exposures to particulate matter (PM2.5: 80.7 vs 117.5 {micro}g/m3), carbon monoxide (CO: 1.3 vs 2.0 ppm), and black carbon (BC: 8.6 vs 12.1 {micro}g/m3) and infancy exposures (PM2.5: 36.9 vs 113.2 {micro}g/m3; CO: 0.60 vs 2.2 ppm). Post-trial PM2.5 exposure were similar between arms: 99.9 vs 98.7 {micro}g/m3. We found no statistically significant effect of the intervention on repeated measures of HAZ ({beta} = -0.06, 95% CI: -0.16, 0.03 p=0.204), annual HAZ, stunting, nor severe stunting at any age during the follow-up. There was no statistically significant effect modification by subgroups.  ConclusionDespite substantial reductions in air pollution exposures during the trial, the LPG intervention did not improve growth or reduce stunting risk from ages 2 through 5 years in this multi-country cohort. These findings, consistent with prior results of the lack of effects on growth through 12 months, provide additional evidence that a clean cooking intervention alone may not be sufficient to address childhood stunting in low-resource settings. Future exposure-response analyses will supplement these ITT analyses.
